title: Opinion | How Nepal’s diverse voices are shaping political awakening and responding to modern challenges - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | How Nepal’s diverse voices are shaping political awakening and responding to modern challenges  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
I am struck by the way a diverse group of people have developed their ways of responding to the complex calls of the times in Nepal. They include academics of various kinds, serious and jesting politicians, analysts, diverse media pundits, creative writers, artists, experts, advisors, philanthropists, civil rights activists, dabblers and idlers. It is not possible, even briefly, to capture the diverse ways in which their responses to the changing times and the series of events gripping this country have evolved over time.

The people listed above have developed diverse ways of responding to the calls and addressing the genius of the times. What is striking, however, is that Nepal has experienced unprecedented commotion across historical, geographical, ecological, political, economic, administrative, financial and educational spheres. We can see the diversity and complexity of the problems by looking at their nature and volume, as well as the problems and achievements.

Political issues have dominated discussions, particularly in light of the changes that have taken place over the years. The rise of youth is the single most dominant factor in this country’s politics. The Gen Z uprising of 2025 has become a mantra used to evoke politics today. What is becoming apparent is that it is a global phenomenon.

Youth uprisings in Asian and European countries have become the dominant metaphor of our time. The role of students in sweeping the election and turning the tide of history in Serbia is the latest example of a student uprising in politics. Other youth movements also exist. The recent political shift in Nepal has created challenges that political scientists and senior political thinkers have been discussing in earnest. They have discussed crucial historical points and alternatives. Professor Lokraj Baral examines the waves in the Nepali Congress, to take one example.

The grand narratives of theory and political hegemony are changing. Measuring this change has become an important issue in Nepal, as it is everywhere in the world. How to tell the old from the new is the outstanding question. Let us turn to politics to try to answer this question.

The question of old and new has been profusely pronounced, if not seriously discussed, in Nepal’s political sphere. The parlance that the old is being replaced by the new, and that youths have emerged to take over the leadership of political parties, has become the most touted topic in Nepali politics. Parties, especially left-leaning ones, are grappling with this question of age-related leadership and ideology.

An attempt to revamp old ideals is a natural process, and probably the only way to give continuity to the tradition of leadership and the definition of followers. One question that has emerged as a prominent issue today is not only the nature of leadership but also of the followers, or the audience, of the parties. Their psyche is measured. The erstwhile revolutionaries, for example, now make cool and reality-based assessments of their actions. Some old leaders of the major political parties issue calls, even orders, not to question the leadership structure of the parties.

That would work if the concerned party were in power, as we have seen in some countries where old leaders in power call on people to follow a certain ideological path or set of principles. But that is no longer the case in Nepal. Parties now have to deal not only with familiar ideological questions but also with the algorithmic digital system that some political scholars have started to describe. Newfangled conspiracy theories and apocalyptic imaginaire also draw from the digital system.

All the major political parties that have ruled for many years are no longer in power. So, they are resorting to organising their parties around the principles and theories. The Gen Z movement changed the structure. But it also raised a major question: how to organise a party in power, like the Rastriya Swatantra Party, around leaders and principles. The leaders of this party, which won nearly two-thirds of the seats in Parliament, are dealing with the question of organising party leadership, streamlining the structure of the supporters or followers. This is not an ordinary challenge but an important moment in history. For that reason, it is a big task for the party to carve out a pragmatic structure that reflects what the British philosopher Bertrand Russell often repeated as the binary of ‘leaders and followers’ that may change its shape with the changing times.

But the themes that shook the Nepalis out of complacency are not only political. They are also physical, and they are huge in scale and impact. The most prominent one is the Bhotekoshi flood. Nepal is facing problems of diverse dimensions. These include physical, economic and ecological dimensions—challenges of an entirely human dimension involving management, protection and settlements.

Human dignity is another major question. People in dire straits face the question of maintaining human dignity and livelihood. The question of management is linked to politics. I like discussions in responsible media that link human topics to the political changes the country has experienced. This involves personas, their actions, behaviours and ethical dimensions. But there are celebratory sides too. Take the festive mood brought by the third season of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) taking place at Tribhuvan University International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur. For someone like me, who has spent my life teaching there, seeing the euphoric crowds is a welcome surprise. That also brings to mind the university’s history and the difficulties this noble institution has faced over time.

title: Opinion | Nepal has the creativity and talent to build its own industries. What it needs is government support - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Nepal has the creativity and talent to build its own industries. What it needs is government support  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
These days, if you are so inclined and have the means, you can be dressed head to toe in thoughtfully designed, sustainable apparel, all made in Nepal. If you are a woman, your jewellery would be made here — traditional, fusion or cutting-edge stuff crafted by recent Kathmandu University BFA graduates. For men, too, there are hand-tooled, embossed leather belts, cufflinks, shoes, T-shirts, and natural fibre button-downs. Work-out and adventure gear for all genders are available for the conservative and the wild.

All your food could be locally sourced, and your toiletries, including your bamboo-made toothbrush with charcoal-stained bristles. Luxuries like homegrown, hand-loomed silk saris, the finest quality pashmina and cashmere shawls, sweaters, gloves, winter hats, and Gurkha-coveted Nepali tweed woven from local wool are all here for those who are interested in buying domestically produced items.

The main issue with accessing most of these remarkable items is pricing, followed by distribution platforms. Most Micro, Medium and Small Enterprises (MSMEs) are working with small margins and high-priced source ingredients, without economies of scale. Additionally, there is little aid from the State, and often unfriendly tax rules that discourage, instead of support, Nepal-made goods. So prices remain high and are often geared for export, as this is the only way such companies with high intellectual property (IP) value and high-cost production can survive.

Nepal is full of would-be entrepreneurs: people who want to start a pickle making business based on their mother’s and grandmother’s recipes, women who knit and embroider and want to make more than just pocket money, some who want to make furniture or start an organic farm, youth who want to write and tell stories in their native languages to make a living, others who want to start small publishing houses for local writers in indigenous languages, and musicians who make their own instruments out of local wood and sell them.

The main hurdle here is the labyrinth of bureaucracy involved in opening such enterprises, along with the opacity, the unfriendliness, the corruption, the paperwork, in difficult, formal Nepali that is a second language to some, not to mention the real dangers of defaulting on hard-to-understand tax filings after registration, resulting in such high fines that will eventually, inevitably, drag a small business under.

Nepal struggles with employment, even more so with meaningful employment. We talk about FDI for large infrastructure projects like mixed use storage and hydropower dams costing billions, which we urgently need for enhancing our own expertise as well as for water security, electricity generation, export and balance of trade. However, to truly bring parity, Nepal must make it easier for people from across disciplines, abilities, genders, ethnic groups and income strata to start businesses, gain access to finance, and, most importantly, be able to unlock government support when it comes to the fundamental tools required to run a business.

There are depressing reports from the financial sector that indicate that micro-credit loans, prioritised by the government for women and the marginalised, often default. This is a major failure on the part of the lenders as well as the government. Not to mention, it is bad for the future of this kind of crucial lending.

Every female advisor we spoke to while drafting our civil society-led Policy Brief on how this government can use existing policies across the education, culture, tourism, commerce and industry and foreign policy sectors to support the Creative Economy said the same thing: policies exist, but enactment and essential corollary support is lacking. The government cannot keep saying there are policies that benefit women who start businesses without actually providing tools with which these women can run these enterprises. Without this kind of support, MSMEs become debt and tax traps.

Development professionals, macro-economists, creatives who want to start businesses, tech people, designers and writers all recognise the need to invest in intellectual property. However, when it comes to practicalities, the country is falling short. Goodwill seems to be present at top leadership, but confusion, lack of education and coordination continue at bureaucratic levels, compounded by natural disasters, world wars, and lack of access to basic business skills which must be introduced at school level.

Nurturing home-grown industries, and tending to the Made in Nepal brand is not easy. Ideas pervade; Nepalis are essentially creative people. Government coordination across the education sector for vocational and business training, and access to learning about local cultures to feed home-grown businesses would revolutionise the landscape for young, would-be entrepreneurs.

Incentivising the tourism industry to pivot towards highlighting local culture for strengthening grass-roots businesses like community homestays, artisanal gift shops and regional cuisine-based eateries is essential. The added benefits of soft power and diplomacy via vibrant culture-based tourism seem both obvious and intuitive, and yet it is like pulling teeth in terms of actual execution. To allow for MSMEs across sectors to have a real shot requires Nepal’s various line ministries to see the bigger picture and coordinate across sectors instead of working in silos.

Manufacturing in Nepal is a must if we are to break away from a remittance-dependent economy. The spectacles that I wear are made out of eco-acetate, and are designed and made in Nepal. There are now at least two different businesses that make international-standard spectacles and sunglasses in Nepal. These could, with the right support, be expanded to become a much bigger industry. Italy is home to EssilorLuxottica, a behemoth in the sunglasses industry. They make sunglasses from brands such as RayBan, Bulgari, Gucci and Persol. The business is worth $91.5 billion, and employs over 200,000 people.

There is no reason why such an industry cannot exist in Nepal. Even more important is the need to nurture industries that are completely vertically integrated so that no raw materials need to be imported. It may seem impossible to develop a textile industry in Nepal against giants like neighbouring Bangladesh, India, China, and even Sri Lanka, but Nepal can and does grow its very own hardy, indigenous variety of cotton.

There were government-supported projects in parts of the country for cotton farming that have now been defunded due to lack of a market and challenges in supply chains; similarly with silk farms, of which only a few remain. Nepal can also harvest kullu , the soft yak down that can easily compete with cashmere (usually imported from Mongolia) in both buttery softness and warmth, but the few people who are trying to do these things cannot get any financing and are stymied by declining herds, low harvests, no subsidies, and transportation bottlenecks.

title: Nepal and Bhutan propose dedicated COP31 agenda on 1.5°C warming in mountain regions - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal and Bhutan propose dedicated COP31 agenda on 1.5°C warming in mountain regions  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal and Bhutan have jointly proposed the inclusion of a dedicated agenda item titled “1.5°C Warming in Mountains” at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, calling for stronger international action to address the escalating impacts of climate change on mountain ecosystems and communities.

In a formal submission addressed to the COP president, incoming COP president and executive secretary of the UNFCCC, the two Himalayan countries have urged the inclusion of the proposed agenda item in the supplementary provisional agenda of COP31. The Post has obtained a copy of a letter sent by Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary.

“On behalf of the Government of Nepal and the Royal Government of Bhutan, I have the honour to submit, in accordance with Rule 12 of the draft Rules of Procedure of the Conference of the Parties, a proposal for the inclusion of a supplementary provisional agenda item entitled “1.5°C Warming in Mountains” at the thirty-first session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), to be held in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026,” reads the letter sent by Chaudhary.

The proposal highlights the growing scientific evidence of accelerated warming in mountain regions, particularly the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH), and warns that rising temperatures are threatening glaciers, biodiversity, water security, food systems, energy production and the livelihoods of millions of people.

The submission argues that mountain ecosystems require greater institutional recognition within the global climate negotiation process, given their critical role in sustaining human populations and maintaining ecological balance.

Mountain regions are warming rapidly, exposing glaciers, snow cover, permafrost and fragile ecosystems to increasingly severe and potentially irreversible changes. The proposal warns that such changes could push adaptation capacities beyond their limits, threatening mountain communities, critical infrastructure and regional economies. The submission emphasises that mountain ecosystems are indispensable to global environmental stability and human well-being.

Mountains serve as the sources of major river systems, supplying freshwater to more than two billion people across Asia and beyond. According to the joint submission, these river systems are essential to water, food, energy and health security, connecting mountain ecosystems with downstream populations and coastal regions.

Mountain regions also cover nearly a quarter of the Earth's surface, support approximately 15 percent of the global population and contain around 50 percent of the world's biodiversity hotspots. Beyond their ecological significance, mountains preserve indigenous cultures, traditional knowledge, unique languages and community-based adaptation practices, the two South Asian nations said.

The proposal underscores the interdependence between upstream and downstream communities, highlighting how changes in glaciers, snowpack and permafrost can affect downstream water availability, agricultural production, hydropower generation and disaster risks.

Mountain ecosystems, particularly those of the Hindu-Kush Himalaya and other high-mountain regions, face growing risks of extreme weather events, reads the letter jointly sent by Nepal and Bhutan.

These impacts endanger the lives and livelihoods of mountain communities and carry far-reaching consequences for the water, food, energy and economic security of billions of people living downstream. The growing frequency and severity of climate-induced disasters further underscore the urgent need for enhanced adaptation, strengthened transboundary cooperation, and equitable access to climate finance and support for loss and damage, reads the letter.

The proposal draws its legal foundation from the preamble and Article 4.8 of the UNFCCC, which recognise the specific needs and vulnerabilities of countries with fragile ecosystems, including mountain ecosystems. It also aligns with international commitments on sustainable mountain development, including Chapter 13 of Agenda 21, United Nations General Assembly Resolution A/RES/71/234 and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030.

The proposal is grounded in the obligations and principles of the Convention, in particular its Preamble and Article 4.8, and bases its observations on the relevant assessments of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the outcomes of recent UNFCCC negotiations, and the political momentum generated by the Sagarmatha Sambad and its Sagarmatha Call for Action of May 2025. It further seeks to advance the outcomes of COP30 and of the Dialogue on Mountains and Climate Change convened in June earlier this year.

Nepal and Bhutan propose that COP31 consider advancing scientific understanding of the impacts and risks of 1.5°C warming and of potential temperature overshoot in mountain regions; institutionalising an annual high-level dialogue on mountains and climate change; initiating a process towards a dedicated UNFCCC Work Programme on Mountain Ecosystems; and integrating mountain-specific priorities into adaptation frameworks, climate finance arrangements and loss and damage mechanisms.

The proposal stresses that a dedicated agenda item could strengthen the collective response of the international community to mountain-related climate risks, and foster solidarity between upstream and downstream countries.

Nepal and Bhutan have expressed their readiness to engage constructively and in a spirit of consultation with all parties, the presidency and the secretariat.

The declaration of 2025 as the International Year of Glaciers' Preservation and the International Decade of Action for Cryospheric Sciences (2025–2034) further demonstrates the growing international recognition of the importance of protecting mountain and glacier systems, the document states.

Citing findings from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, including the Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate and the Sixth Assessment Report, the submission stresses the urgent need to limit global warming to 1.5°C and avoid temperature overshoot.

It calls for stronger transboundary cooperation, coordinated disaster risk reduction, improved early warning systems and systematic data sharing among countries sharing mountain river basins.

Recent disasters in Nepal, including the Melamchi floods in 2021, the Kathmandu and Thame events in 2024, the Ilam disaster in 2025 and the Bhote Koshi catastrophe in 2026, demonstrate the growing exposure of mountain communities and infrastructure to extreme rainfall, floods, landslides and cryosphere-related hazards.

The submission highlights the Bhote Koshi disaster as a particularly serious example of the economic consequences of climate vulnerability in mountainous developing countries.

Citing Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the proposal states that $4.7 billion, equivalent to around 10 percent of the country’s gross domestic product, would be needed for the reconstruction of property and infrastructure damaged in the flash flood triggered by a glacier collapse.

The countries argue that these events demonstrate the urgent need for enhanced adaptation measures, risk-informed development, regional cooperation and equitable access to climate finance, particularly funding for addressing loss and damage.

They also emphasise that the impacts of climate change extend beyond economic losses, affecting cultural heritage, traditional livelihoods, indigenous knowledge and the social fabric of vulnerable mountain communities.

In the proposed agenda item, Nepal and Bhutan have identified four major areas for consideration by the international climate community. Advancing scientific understanding of 1.5°C overshoot in mountains; institutionalising an annual High-Level Dialogue on Mountains and Climate Change and m o untain-related priorities within the UNFCCC process; establishing a dedicated UNFCCC Mountain Work Programme and integrating mountain priorities into global climate finance and adaptation frameworks.

title: Nepal cancels tender for Sunkoshi Marin dam and power plant — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal cancels tender for Sunkoshi Marin dam and power plant — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal has cancelled the tender procedure for a contract to build a dam and power plant for the Sunkoshi Marin multipurpose project. The decision was made several days before the planned opening of financial proposals from three companies that passed technical selection, Kathmandu Post reports.

Senior project engineer Ashok Raj Gautam said the procedure was cancelled on the instruction of the Department of Water Resources and Irrigation. According to him, the department must decide whether to announce a new tender or choose another course of action. He did not explain the reasons for the cancellation.

Final stage of the competition

International competitive bidding was announced on June 8, giving potential contractors 30 days to submit proposals. Six construction companies took part.

China International Water and Electric Corporation, Anneng-RCC JV and Sinohydro Corporation Limited of China advanced to the final stage. Their financial proposals were scheduled to be opened on Monday, but this will not happen following the cancellation of the procedure.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Project delays

The Sunkoshi Marin project is intended to provide year-round irrigation for 122,000 hectares of agricultural land in five Terai districts — Bara, Rautahat, Sarlahi, Mahottari and Dhanusha. It also provides for the generation of 31.07 MW of electricity.

A previous contract worth 14.07 billion rupees was awarded in January 2023 to Patel-Raman JV, a joint venture comprising India’s Patel Engineering and Nepal’s Raman Construction. The agreement was terminated on November 11, 2025, due to insufficient progress: after 60% of the allotted period had elapsed, physical work completion did not exceed 11%.

The project includes a dam about 30 metres high and 158 metres long on the Sunkoshi River and the diversion of water through a tunnel to the Marin River in Sindhuli district. The 13.3-km tunnel has already been completed and tested, but it cannot be commissioned without the dam. Under the revised master plan, the entire project is to be completed in the 2032–33 fiscal year.

title: LDC Graduation Deferred - The Rising Nepal
description: LDC Graduation Deferred  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Nepal has been under the category of least developed country (LDC) since the United Nations General Assembly in 1971 created the group to represent low-income countries which are highly vulnerable to economic and environmental shocks and possess low levels of human assets. There were 25 LDCs, including Nepal, in 1971, which later peaked at 51 in 2003. So far, nine countries that once fell under the LDC category have exited the group, and there now remain 44 countries in the group. As per the provision of the UN to provide preferential treatment to LDCs, Nepal has been enjoying targeted support from the international community, such as preferential trade access, development financing and technical assistance.





Following remarkable progress in two criteria—Human Assets Index and Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index—except Per Capita GNI, out of the three criteria set for LDC graduation, Nepal initially planned to graduate from the LDC category in 2018, which was later deferred due to the massive economic turmoil caused by the 2015 earthquake. The COVID-19 pandemic also forced the country to defer its graduation plan, set for 2021, for the second time. Currently, as per the official request of the Government of Nepal, the United Nations General Assembly has unanimously adopted a proposal to extend the preparatory period for Nepal's graduation from LDC status by three years, from 24 November 2026 to 24 November 2029.





The latest extension of the time for LDC graduation has brought relief to Nepal while the national economy has been severely affected by recent political changes in the country caused by the Gen Z movement, disruptions in the global supply chain after the US-Iran war, and the recent catastrophic flash floods. This extension has given three more years to Nepal to make necessary preparations for sustainable and irreversible graduation, and build a resilient economy to cope with post-graduation circumstances. After the extension of the LDC graduation deadline, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said that the country will use the period to enhance productive capacity, strengthen institutions and advance economic and social transformation. The ministry further stated that Nepal will also focus on the effective implementation of its Smooth Transition Strategy, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Doha Programme of Action to ensure a smooth transition after graduation.





Meanwhile, the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI) has welcomed the decision to extend Nepal’s preparatory period for graduation. The FNCCI had long been urging an extension of the preparatory period, expressing concern that graduating without adequate improvements in productive capacity, industrial infrastructure, technology, productivity and quality could adversely affect Nepali industries, exports and employment.





Despite the preferential treatment provided by the international community in trade, financing and technical assistance under the LDC category, Nepal's economy is not performing well, mainly due to its low production base, lack of quality goods, high production costs and infrastructural bottlenecks. As a result, the country has been unable to increase and diversify its exports and is relying heavily on imports, even for products that have high potential for domestic production. In this situation, the extension of the LDC graduation period was essential to minimise the potential risks to the economy in the post-graduation scenario.





However, the three-year extension of the LDC graduation timeline should not be seen as a cause for celebration. Remaining in the LDC category for more than 45 years is a matter of concern and does little to enhance Nepal’s standing and dignity in the international community. The government and the business sector must, therefore, make effective use of this additional time to ensure Nepal’s sustainable and irreversible graduation in 2029.

title: Preventing Burn Injuries During Tihar - The Rising Nepal
description: Preventing Burn Injuries During Tihar  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
We are approaching one of the most celebrated festivals in Nepal, i.e., Tihar, also known as Dipawali. During this festival, homes are decorated with oil lamps, candles, rangolis, and colourful lights. Families also enjoy fireworks and firecrackers to add excitement to this festival. It is commonly called as festival of joy and symbolizes the victory of good over evil, Tihar, therefore, should be celebrated cautiously and responsibly.

Issue

The excitement also brings the danger of burn injuries, particularly to children and young adults while handling firecrackers, candles, oil lamps, and other flammable materials. It is, therefore, important to celebrate this festival safely in order to avoid burn injuries. The careless handling of these flammable materials has been causing burn injuries every year, particularly to young children. Male predominance is seen with firecracker injuries, while females suffer oil lamp-related burns.

The improper use of fireworks and firecrackers can cause burn injuries to people, especially children, as they are more attracted to bright lights and loud sounds. Unexpectedly exploded firecrackers can cause serious burns to the hands, face, eyes, and other parts of the body. Sometimes, adults may be the victim of fireworks owing to overconfidence or negligence. It is, therefore, essential for parents and guardians to supervise while handling fireworks by their children. Nevertheless, children should be educated about the risks associated with firecrackers and asked to avoid holding crackers in their hands and relighting fireworks that failed to explode.

The unsafe use of traditional oil lamps, candles, and diyas has been causing burn injuries predominantly to female children and sometimes even adult females. These items can cause fires if placed near curtains, wooden furniture, or other combustible articles. It is, thus, essential to place oil lamps or diyas on stable, non-flammable surfaces and keep them away from curtains and other combustible materials. Candles and oil lamps should not be left unattended when children or pets are present in the house. It is important to extinguish candles and oil lamps before sleeping or leaving the house.

Clothing is another concern for burn injuries. Children and young adults wear new and attractive clothes during this festival, and clothes made from synthetic materials such as nylon and polyester can catch fire easily and also melt when hot. It is, therefore, essential to avoid loose-fitting clothes and wear well-fitted cotton fabric while lighting lamps or enjoying fireworks. Long scarves, traditional long shawls, and loose sleeves should be avoided while engaging in lighting lamps or fireworks or open flames. Hence, simple precautions can prevent burn injuries and protect people from unwanted suffering.

Moreover, public awareness and education to children is important to prevent burn injuries, particularly during Dipawali. It is essential to impart knowledge on fire safety measures by schools, colleges, hospitals, local governments, and community organizations through radio, television, newspapers, and social media before Dipawali. The awareness campaign should include safe handling of fireworks, the proper use of oil lamps, fire prevention measures, and first aid for burns. The campaign related to fire safety measures should not be limited to a few days before the festival but should be a regular part of health education programs.

The availability of first-aid kits is also important during the festival. Despite every precaution, accidents may still occur. Hence, it is important for every household to know how to respond when burn injuries occur. The affected part of the body should be placed under running cool water for about 20-30 minutes and avoid ice, butter, oil, or other household products. It is suggested to remove any clothing or jewellery near the burned area, provided it is not stuck to the skin and loosely cover the burn with a non-fluffy dressing or cloth. Serious burns, particularly of the face and injuries to children, should be brought to prompt medical attention.

Local governments and communities have an important role in public safety during Dipawali. Firecrackers should be used only in designated open spaces and far from buildings, vehicles, petrol station, and crowded areas. It is important for emergency medical services and hospitals to remain alert to treat burn-related emergencies during Dipawali. Local governments should strictly monitor the sale and use of highly dangerous fireworks. After all, public safety is more important than entertainment or profit.

It is time to debate whether fireworks are necessary for celebrating Dipawali or not. Fireworks not only have the potential to cause burn injuries but also cause noise and air pollution, and cause health problems, particularly to children, elderly, and people having respiratory ailments. It is, thus, important to celebrate this festival with safer and more environmentally friendly approaches. Dipawali can be celebrated with decorative colourful lights, traditional lamps, traditional cultural programs such as Deusi and Vailo, family gatherings, and community events.

Conclusion

Children often imitate adults; therefore, parents have an important role during the festival. Parents and guardians should always practice a safe approach and teach their children about the precautions so that children develop safe habits related to the celebrations. Let us celebrate the festival of lights with happiness, family gatherings, and responsible eating of sugary food and drinks. By preventing burn injuries, we can prevent severe physical pain, emotional distress, permanent scarring, and, of course, financial burden. Let us celebrate this festival by illuminating our homes and hearts, thereby preventing ourselves and others from unnecessary suffering and distress.

(Dr. Shyam P Lohani is the clinical director at the Nepal Poison Information Centre. lohanis@gmail.com)

title: Nationalism, Foreign Policy And Sovereignty - The Rising Nepal
description: Nationalism, Foreign Policy And Sovereignty  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
One of the oldest nations, Nepal is a civilisational state. The enlightenment tradition, grounded in Vedic knowledge, King Janak's spiritual and critical discourse, and Buddha's rationalist philosophy, has guided Nepalis' worldviews and collective consciousness. Hindu philosophy is so broad that it even embraced the materialistic school of Charvak. Cosmopolitan vision, solidarity and compassion have characterised Nepali society and political culture. Nepal has sheltered all types of refugees -- political, ethnic, royal, and religious -- since time immemorial. This is why Nepal's motto of foreign policy is: Amity with all, and enmity with none.

So are Nepali nationalism and patriotism, shaped by ancient wisdom and shared humanity. Its source is national independence, resistance to colonisation, syncretic culture, religious tolerance, national geography and the willingness of people to stay with their nationality. Before and after the unification, our valiant ancestors had demonstrated an indomitable spirit against the foreign invaders. They fought the Mughals, Chinese imperial rulers and the British to defend territorial sovereignty and integrity. The old concept of nationalism is rooted in ethnic nationality or ethnos, based on tribal hierarchy of humans but democracy is based on demos: equal citizens with equal rights and duties. Our patriotism and nationalism transcend territorial boundaries and include Nepali society all over the world. They uphold Nepali identity but are citizens of various countries and emotionally support Nepal in troubled times. Nepaliness is defined by its culture, not antagonism against a particular country or religion.

Geopolitical interest

Nepali nationalism should not be defined based on an insular outlook. If nationalism is used to meet vested personal or geopolitical interests, the idea that serves as a rallying cry to unite the people will lose its relevance. Now the debate on nationalism has received renewed focus after Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle, speaking at a Nepal-India relations event at the NDTV World Summit recently, argued that ‘there was a time when nationalism in Nepal was associated with anti-India sentiment. But that era is now over.’ FM Wagle’s remark has stirred a hornet’s nest at home, triggering arguments and counter-arguments in support of and against it. He was apparently referring to Nepali left forces known for an acerbic stance on India’s treatment of the Himalayan nation. His loathing of communists is clear. He is inveighing against them as they are on the defensive. But belligerent ideological posturing has little place in diplomacy.

FM’s strong statement raises a volley of questions: is Nepali nationalism confined to anti-Indian feelings? Are there no historical factors spurring this kind of situation? Will Dr. Wagle’s view help build a common stand on Nepal’s foreign policy? Won’t his ideologically charged statement overshadow the pressing economic and trade issues involving Nepal and India? There should be a consensus approach to foreign policy, with all domestic forces coming to common ground. Unfortunately, there has been politicisation of Nepal’s foreign policy devoid of reasoned debate and geopolitical reality.

Nepal’s foreign policy has been guided by the constitution, the principle of Panchsheel, non-alignment policy, the UN Charter and bilateral and multilateral agreements. Sometime back, while giving an interview to The Rising Nepal, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said that there would be continuity in foreign policy. This clearly implies that the government will not set aside pertinent issues that irritate Nepal-India relations. Border disputes in several places, including Kalapani, Lipulek and Limpiyadhura, the 1950 treaty, the EPG report, regulation of the border and trade obstacles have often beset the bilateral relations between the two countries. FM Khanal’s statement suggested that the present government would not abandon these matters. Failure to resolve the vexing bilateral subjects has, of course, given rise to anti-Indian sentiment in Nepal. But raising these issues does not necessarily make one anti-Indian. Neither is anti-Indian sentiment the core ingredient of Nepali nationalism.

Nepal and India have historical, cultural, religious, social and economic ties. People-to-people relations between the two nations are sound. The disputes at the highest political level do not affect this bond. The attempts at micromanaging internal affairs of another country always backfire in the long run. Hence both neighbours must reset ties in the changed context, focusing on developmental diplomacy and mutual prosperity.

Art of statecraft

Diplomacy is an art of statecraft to advance national interest and enhance ties with the neighbours and friendly nations. Internal unity is necessary to muster the support of the international community. A responsible leader does not spill the domestic beans in foreign land. This will only weaken the national position to negotiate with foreign countries. The language of mockery, underestimation, and sycophancy has no place in the diction of diplomacy. Balanced expression, dignified conduct and result-oriented work ensure diplomatic success.

With almost two-thirds majority, the present government is in a good position to bolster Nepal's nationalism, sovereignty, and right to self-determination. Upon his election to the highest executive office, Prime Minister Balendra Shah has stressed good governance, corruption control, policy reforms, a diplomatic code of conduct, the principle of equality and a self-reliant economy. His priority of reviving the sick industries demonstrates that the new government aspires to attain economic independence and prosperity – the lynchpin of nationalism. Freedom, sovereignty, geographical integrity and protection of national interest form the basis of our nationalism. Nepalis have pinned high hopes on Prime Minister Shah that he will effectively articulate these cardinal values of the Nepali state when he visits India in the near future.





(The author is the Managing Editor of this daily.)

title: Six Indian Tourists Go Missing While Trekking in Nepal - Deccan Chronicle
description: Six Indian Tourists Go Missing While Trekking in Nepal  Deccan Chronicle
publisher.title: Deccan Chronicle
full_article:
The missing tourists, comprising two women and four men, were travelling from Ward Nos. 4 and 8 of Dolpo Buddha Rural Municipality towards Shey-Phoksundo Lake.

They were last reported missing in the Numla Pass and Bagla Pass areas between Ward Nos. 4 and 8 of Shey-Phoksundo Rural Municipality.

Local guides suspect that the tourists may have become stranded following heavy snowfall in the Himalayan region, reportedly influenced by Cyclone Arnab developing over the Bay of Bengal.

According to local officials, the tourists continued towards the high-altitude region despite warnings from residents about difficult weather conditions and the risks of crossing the mountain passes.

They are believed to have become trapped in the snow while returning from their journey.

Dolpa Chief District Officer Junu Hamal confirmed that “the tourists became stranded while returning from Dho towards Phoksundo Lake.”

She further said, “They had been warned by locals about the difficult weather and mountain conditions but proceeded with their journey.”

Shey-Phoksundo Rural Municipality Chairman Dhawa Samduk Gurung said mobile phone communication was unavailable in the mountain passes between Wards 4 and 8, making it difficult to obtain information about the tourists' whereabouts and current condition.

According to the District Administration Office, a total of 244 tourists have reached Upper Dolpa. Of these, 149 are Nepali nationals, 44 are from SAARC countries and 51 are citizens of other foreign countries.

In view of the adverse weather conditions, the district administration has urged tourists to avoid risky areas and remain in safe locations.

Tourist arrivals in the Shey-Phoksundo Lake region have been increasing in recent years. According to available data, 4,882 tourists visited Phoksundo Lake during the first 11 months of the fiscal year 2082/83.

Dolpa Deputy Superintendent of Police Anil Raj Giri said six Indian tourists remained uncontactable, according to the latest information.

He added that authorities had requested the concerned agency to arrange a helicopter for search and rescue operations.

Search and rescue efforts have been hampered by heavy snowfall and adverse weather conditions in the high Himalayan region.

The absence of mobile phone connectivity and thick snow have further complicated efforts to establish the tourists' whereabouts and assess their condition.

A team of the Nepal Army has also been deployed to locate the missing tourists and assist in rescue operations.

title: Nepal court says loan misuse can warrant investigation - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal court says loan misuse can warrant investigation  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal’s Supreme Court has ruled that using a loan for purposes other than those intended may constitute grounds for a criminal investigation under banking legislation, even if the borrower regularly pays the principal, interest and installments. At the same time, the court stressed that the mere fact of alleged misuse of funds does not automatically mean a person is found guilty — the circumstances must be supported by evidence and examined during court proceedings.

As reported by the Kathmandu Post, the ruling was issued on July 30, 2026, by a panel of judges Tek Prasad Dungana and Meghraj Pokhrel. It concerned a habeas corpus petition challenging the legality of the detention, filed on behalf of Prabhu Bank borrower Shashidhar Sharma. The court dismissed the petition but did not make a final determination as to whether he had in fact used the loan funds in breach of the terms.

Regulator’s inspection

On January 17, 2025, Sharma obtained a 480 million rupee loan from Prabhu Bank to buy land for a resort in Rupandehi. According to a special on-site inspection by the central bank, Nepal Rastra Bank, the funds were not used for their stated purpose.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

According to the court’s account, the money was transferred to accounts of persons linked to Sharma and then to other individuals and institutions. Part of the funds, according to the inspection, was used to repay loans of other companies owned by the same person. On July 14, 2026, Nepal Rastra Bank sent the report to the Central Investigation Bureau of Nepal Police, after which law enforcement began an investigation under Article 8 of the Banking Offence and Punishment Act 2008 and detained Sharma.

Risks for lending

The court noted that neither a complaint from the lending bank nor a prior demand for the borrower to return the funds was required to launch an investigation. It also stated that Nepal Rastra Bank had lawful authority to forward the inspection findings to the body authorized to investigate the case. At the same time, the court cautioned against unjustified detention: when extending detention, the stage of the investigation, the necessity of such a measure and the grounds for it should be assessed.

Bankers said that this interpretation of the law could weaken lending. Nepal Bankers’ Association President Santosh Koirala said that in the past loans were often used for purposes other than those approved, and some of these funds are still tied up in investments. According to him, the banking system already has excess liquidity, historically low interest rates and weak demand for loans.
